items.title: [Real Estate 101 #14] Your Property Sends You Two Tax Bills — One Every Year, One Only Once
items.body:
> Owning real estate means paying tax while you hold it and tax when you sell it — and good management is largely the work of shrinking both without shrinking the asset.

## Today's Concept

Most people think of a property as a thing you buy. In practice it's a small business you run, and like any business it has an operating side and a tax side.

**The operating side: property management vs. asset management.**

*Property management* is the day-to-day: finding tenants, collecting rent, fixing the water heater at 11 p.m., handling turnovers, keeping the building code-compliant. In the U.S., a residential property manager typically charges **8–10% of collected rent**, often plus a leasing fee of half to one month's rent each time a unit turns over.

*Asset management* is the level above it: Should we hold or sell? Refinance? Spend $40,000 on a kitchen renovation to push rents, or spend nothing and harvest cash? Property management protects the income; asset management decides what the income is *for*.

Both are measured through one number: **Net Operating Income (NOI)**.

```
NOI = effective gross income − operating expenses
```

Operating expenses include property taxes, insurance, maintenance, management fees, and utilities you cover. They **exclude** your mortgage payment and depreciation. That's deliberate — NOI describes the property, not your financing.

**The tax side: two very different bills.**

**1) The annual bill — property tax (the "holding tax").** In the U.S. this is levied locally, not federally: by counties, cities, and school districts. The county assessor sets an *assessed value*, and a tax rate (often quoted in *mills* — dollars per $1,000 of value) is applied to it. Effective rates vary enormously — roughly 0.3% of market value in Hawaii to well over 2% in New Jersey and parts of Illinois and Texas. On the same $400,000 house, that's the difference between about $1,200 and $8,800 a year, every year, forever.

Two things worth knowing: most states offer a **homestead exemption** that reduces the taxable value of your primary residence, and every state has a formal **assessment appeal** process. Some states also cap how fast assessed value can rise — California's Proposition 13 limits the increase to 2% per year until the property sells, at which point it's reassessed at market value.

**2) The one-time bill — capital gains tax (the "transfer tax").** When you sell, you're taxed on the *gain*, not the sale price:

```
gain = amount realized (sale price − selling costs) − adjusted basis
adjusted basis = purchase price + capital improvements − depreciation taken
```

Hold longer than one year and the gain gets **long-term capital gains** rates (0%, 15%, or 20% federally, depending on income), plus a possible 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax at higher incomes, plus state tax. Sell within a year and it's taxed as ordinary income — a materially worse outcome.

**The wrinkle that surprises everyone: depreciation recapture.** While you own a rental, the IRS lets you deduct the *building* (never the land) over **27.5 years** for residential property or **39 years** for commercial — a paper expense that shelters real cash income. But at sale, the depreciation you took gets pulled back into the gain as *unrecaptured Section 1250 gain*, taxed at up to 25%. Depreciation is a deferral, not a gift. And here's the trap: the IRS computes recapture on depreciation "allowed or allowable" — you owe it whether or not you actually claimed the deduction.

Three legal off-ramps are worth knowing by name:

- **Section 121 exclusion** — sell your *primary residence* after living in it 2 of the last 5 years and exclude up to **$250,000** of gain (single) or **$500,000** (married filing jointly).
- **Section 1031 like-kind exchange** — on *investment* property, roll the proceeds into another investment property and defer the gain. Strict clock: identify replacement property within **45 days**, close within **180 days**, and a qualified intermediary must hold the money. Since 2018 this applies to real property only.
- **Step-up in basis at death** — heirs generally inherit at fair market value, which can erase decades of embedded gain.

## In Everyday Life

Say you buy a single-family rental in Columbus, Ohio for **$300,000**. The county allocates $60,000 to land and $240,000 to the building. You put $150,000 down and borrow $150,000 at 6.5%.

**Year one, the operating side:**

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Gross rent ($2,200 × 12) | $26,400 |
| Less vacancy (5%) | −$1,320 |
| **Effective gross income** | **$25,080** |
| Property tax | −$4,500 |
| Insurance | −$1,400 |
| Management (9%) | −$2,257 |
| Repairs & maintenance | −$2,000 |
| **NOI** | **$14,923** |

Your mortgage costs about $948/month, or $11,377/year. So your actual **cash flow is about $3,546**.

**Now the tax side of the same year:**

```
NOI                          $14,923
− mortgage interest          $ 9,700   (principal is not deductible)
− depreciation ($240k/27.5)  $ 8,727
= taxable rental income     −$ 3,504
```

You put roughly $3,500 of cash in your pocket and report a **$3,500 loss**. That gap is depreciation doing its job. (Whether you can *use* that loss is a separate question — rental losses are generally "passive," though there's a special allowance of up to $25,000 for active participants, which phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of modified AGI.)

One nice detail: property taxes on a *rental* are an ordinary business expense on Schedule E and are **not** subject to the SALT cap that limits state and local tax deductions on your personal return. The same dollar of property tax is treated very differently depending on whether you live in the house or rent it out.

**Ten years later, you sell for $400,000** with 6% selling costs:

```
Amount realized    $400,000 − $24,000 = $376,000
Depreciation taken $8,727 × 10        = $ 87,270
Adjusted basis     $300,000 − $87,270 = $212,730
Total gain                              $163,270
   of which $87,270 is recapture       (up to 25%)
   and      $76,000 is long-term gain  (0/15/20%)
```

Notice: the property appreciated $100,000, but your taxable gain is $163,270. The extra $63,000-odd is the bill for ten years of depreciation deductions coming due — which is precisely why 1031 exchanges exist.

## Three-Line Recap

1. Property management protects NOI day to day; asset management decides when to hold, improve, refinance, or sell.
2. Property tax is local, annual, and permanent — effective rates range from under 0.5% to over 2% of value, so the *location* of a purchase is also a tax decision.
3. Capital gains tax is computed on gain over adjusted basis, and depreciation lowers that basis — so the deduction you enjoy while holding is largely a deferral you settle at sale.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**1.** Which of the following is **excluded** from operating expenses when calculating NOI?
  a) Property taxes   b) Property management fees   c) Mortgage principal and interest   d) Landlord-paid insurance

**2.** True or False: Residential rental buildings are depreciated over 27.5 years, and the land is depreciated over the same period.

**3.** You bought a rental for $300,000, made $20,000 of capital improvements, and took $50,000 of depreciation. What is your adjusted basis?
  a) $230,000   b) $270,000   c) $300,000   d) $370,000

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **NOI (Net Operating Income)** — Effective gross income minus operating expenses, before financing and depreciation; the standard measure of a property's earning power.
- **Assessed value / mill rate** — The value a local assessor assigns to a property, and the tax rate applied to it, quoted as dollars per $1,000 of value.
- **Adjusted basis** — Purchase price plus capital improvements minus depreciation taken; the number your sale proceeds are measured against to compute gain.
- **Depreciation recapture (unrecaptured §1250 gain)** — The portion of gain attributable to depreciation you previously deducted, taxed at up to 25% at sale.
- **Section 1031 exchange** — A swap of one investment property for another that defers capital gains tax, subject to 45-day identification and 180-day closing deadlines.

*This is an educational overview of how U.S. real estate taxation is structured, not tax advice. Rates, thresholds, and caps change with legislation and vary by state — confirm current figures with a CPA before acting.*

---

*Answers: 1 — c. NOI deliberately excludes debt service so the property can be compared independently of how it was financed. 2 — False. The 27.5-year schedule applies to the building only; land is never depreciated, which is why the purchase price must be allocated between the two. 3 — b. $300,000 + $20,000 − $50,000 = $270,000; every dollar of depreciation you take lowers your basis and therefore raises your eventual taxable gain.*

items.title: Cyber Privateers: Inside the New Program Letting Vetted US Firms Hack Back at Foreign Scam Networks
items.body:
## A New Kind of Authorization

Earlier this month, the White House quietly signed a presidential memorandum that cybersecurity policy watchers are already comparing to a modern letters-of-marque system. According to summaries of the directive that have circulated among industry and legal analysts, it creates the first formal US framework allowing specially vetted private companies to conduct offensive cyber operations against foreign criminal networks — under federal supervision and within limits set by national security agencies.

Supporters are calling it "cyber privateering," a nod to the historical practice of governments commissioning private ships to act against enemy vessels. The comparison is deliberate: instead of navies and cannons, the tools here are digital — network intrusion, infrastructure disruption, and data recovery aimed at the servers and accounts used by scam operations, ransomware gangs, and fraud rings believed to be operating from outside US borders.

## What the Program Reportedly Does

Based on descriptions from people familiar with the policy, the framework does not hand out blanket permission to "hack back." Instead, it reportedly sets up a structured pipeline:

- **Vetting of companies.** Firms seeking to participate would need to apply through a federal review process, likely involving agencies with cybersecurity and law enforcement mandates, before being authorized to act.
- **Target approval.** Rather than letting companies choose their own targets, officials would reportedly vet and approve specific foreign infrastructure or networks tied to criminal activity before any operation could proceed.
- **Defined limits.** Analysts expect the program to include rules of engagement — restrictions on the scope, duration, and techniques permitted — along with reporting requirements back to federal overseers.

Officials familiar with the effort say the intent is to formalize something that has, in practice, happened informally for years: private threat-intelligence and incident-response firms have occasionally taken disruptive action against criminal infrastructure while operating in a legal gray area. The new program is meant to bring that activity under clearer federal authorization rather than leaving companies to guess at the legal boundaries.

## Why Now: The Scam Epidemic

The timing tracks with a broader push in Washington to respond to the scale of online fraud hitting American consumers. Federal Trade Commission data and industry fraud-tracking reports have repeatedly shown Americans losing billions of dollars annually to romance scams, fake investment platforms, tech-support fraud, and pig-butchering schemes — many of which are run out of scam compounds and criminal networks based overseas, often beyond the practical reach of US law enforcement.

Backers of the new authority argue that traditional tools — indictments, sanctions, and law-enforcement takedown requests routed through foreign governments — have proven too slow and too easily ignored by criminal operations that simply relocate servers or shift jurisdictions. Giving cleared private-sector teams, who often have deeper technical visibility into criminal infrastructure than government agencies do, a lawful path to act is being framed as a way to close that gap.

Industry groups representing cybersecurity firms have generally welcomed the move, saying it could let companies act on threat intelligence they already possess instead of watching criminal networks operate with impunity while paperwork moves through slower government channels.

## The Skeptics' Case

Not everyone is convinced. Cybersecurity researchers and former government officials have raised several concerns publicly and in trade publications since news of the memorandum spread:

- **Escalation risk.** Offensive operations against infrastructure in another country — even infrastructure used by criminals — could be misread as a state-linked act, especially if the targeted network sits inside a country with its own tensions with Washington.
- **Attribution mistakes.** Criminal infrastructure is frequently rented, shared, or spoofed. Critics warn that hitting the wrong server could damage systems belonging to unrelated businesses or ordinary users.
- **Accountability gaps.** Questions remain about who is legally liable if a sanctioned operation causes unintended damage abroad, and how affected foreign governments or companies would seek recourse.
- **Precedent concerns.** Some legal scholars note that authorizing private offensive action, even under supervision, sets a precedent other countries could point to when justifying their own state-tolerated hacking groups.

None of these risks have been tested in practice yet, which is precisely what worries critics — the program is moving from concept to operation before there is a track record showing how vetting, oversight, and damage control would actually function under pressure.

## What Comes Next

The memorandum reportedly leaves significant implementation details — including which agencies will run the vetting process and how disputes or unintended consequences will be handled — to be worked out in follow-up guidance. Congressional staff and cybersecurity policy groups are expected to scrutinize those details closely in the coming weeks, particularly around oversight mechanisms and how "foreign criminal network" will be legally defined.

For now, the program remains more framework than fully operational reality. Whether it becomes an effective new front against the scam economy draining billions from Americans each year — or a source of the international friction skeptics fear — will likely depend on how narrowly the vetting and target-approval process is actually enforced once operations begin.

items.title: The $4,000 School Year: How Tariffs Turned Back-to-School Shopping Into a Debt Decision
items.body:
## A Shopping List That Costs More Than It Used To

For millions of families, the ritual of back-to-school shopping has quietly turned into one of the biggest financial stress tests of the year. Industry surveys tracking household spending now put the average cost of outfitting a single child for the new school year at close to $4,000 once tuition-adjacent costs, clothing, electronics, and everyday supplies are added together. That figure has been climbing for several years, but this season feels different to a lot of parents — and the reason many point to is tariffs.

A wide share of the products that fill a typical school shopping cart — notebooks, backpacks, lunch boxes, sneakers, and basic apparel — are manufactured overseas and imported into the United States. When import tariffs rise on those categories, the added cost doesn't stay with the manufacturer or the importer for long. It tends to move down the supply chain until it lands on a store shelf, and ultimately, in a parent's shopping cart.

## Where the Price Increases Are Showing Up

Retail analysts tracking this back-to-school season say the sharpest increases are concentrated in a handful of categories that were already price-sensitive for families:

- **School supplies** such as notebooks, binders, and basic stationery, many of which are produced in facilities affected by new tariff schedules.
- **Lunch boxes and insulated bags**, a category dominated by imported goods with limited domestic manufacturing alternatives.
- **Clothing and footwear**, where apparel tariffs have compounded with existing cost pressures from labor and shipping.
- **Basic electronics accessories**, including calculators, headphones, and chargers commonly required for middle and high school classes.

Several of these categories are reportedly seeing price increases in the double digits compared to last year, according to retail pricing trackers — a jump that is hard for many household budgets to absorb without some kind of trade-off.

## Nearly Half of Parents Say They'll Borrow to Cover It

What makes this year notable isn't just the price tag — it's how families say they plan to pay for it. Recent consumer surveys suggest that nearly half of parents expect to rely on some form of credit, whether that's a credit card balance carried past the due date, a "buy now, pay later" installment plan, or a short-term loan, just to get through the shopping list.

For financial counselors, that's a meaningful shift. Back-to-school spending has traditionally been treated as a predictable, budgeted expense — closer to a utility bill than a financial emergency. When a routine seasonal purchase starts requiring borrowed money for a large share of households, it's often read as a signal of broader strain on discretionary budgets, not just a one-off spike in school supply prices.

## Why This Year Is Being Called a Turning Point

Economists who track consumer goods pricing note that this may be the first back-to-school season where the majority of a typical shopping list is made up of products directly affected by new tariff policy. In previous years, tariff impacts were more concentrated in specific categories, like electronics or certain apparel segments. This year, the breadth of affected goods — from paper products to footwear — means fewer families have an easy substitution available.

That breadth is part of why the story has resonated beyond typical economic reporting. It isn't an abstract trade statistic; it shows up directly in a parent's total at the register.

## What Families Are Doing Differently

Facing higher prices across nearly every category, many households are adjusting their shopping habits rather than simply absorbing the cost:

- **Buying fewer items per category** and prioritizing what's absolutely required by the school's supply list.
- **Shopping secondhand or swapping** clothing and supplies with other families.
- **Spreading purchases out** across several weeks instead of one large shopping trip, to manage cash flow.
- **Comparing store brands versus name brands** more aggressively than in past years.
- **Using layaway or installment options** at retailers that offer them, rather than defaulting straight to a credit card.

Financial advisors generally caution that while short-term financing tools can help smooth a one-time expense, relying on revolving credit for a recurring annual cost like school shopping can create a cycle that's difficult to break, especially if next year's prices continue trending upward.

## The Bigger Picture

Back-to-school spending is often treated as a bellwether for household financial health heading into the fall and holiday shopping season. If a growing share of families are financing routine purchases this early in the year, that trend is likely to draw closer attention from retailers, lenders, and policymakers alike in the months ahead. For now, though, the immediate reality for many parents is simpler and more pressing: get the list checked off, and figure out how to pay for it later.

items.title: A Coastline Shook Twice in One Day: Inside the Earthquake That Devastated Indonesia's Flores Island
items.body:
A powerful magnitude-7.7 earthquake struck off the coast of Flores Island in eastern Indonesia, killing more than 50 people and injuring hundreds more, according to national disaster officials. The quake, one of the strongest to hit the region in years, was followed by more than 230 aftershocks and, hours later, a second major tremor that shook the island of Sumatra thousands of kilometers away — turning a single day into one of the most severe tests of Indonesia's emergency response systems in recent memory.

## A Sudden, Violent Shock

The initial quake struck without warning, its epicenter located beneath the seabed near Flores, a mountainous island in the Nusa Tenggara region known for its volcanic terrain and small coastal communities. Indonesia's Meteorological, Climatological and Geophysical Agency (BMKG) issued a tsunami advisory in the immediate aftermath, prompting evacuations along low-lying shorelines before the warning was later downgraded.

The shaking was strong enough to collapse older masonry buildings, damage schools and health clinics, and trigger landslides that buried sections of the island's main coastal roads. Officials with Indonesia's National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) reported that thousands of residents were displaced, many now sheltering in temporary camps, mosques, and community halls as search-and-rescue teams work to reach isolated villages.

## Aftershocks Complicate the Response

What has made this disaster especially difficult to manage is the sheer volume of aftershocks that followed — more than 230 by some counts, according to seismic monitoring agencies. Each new tremor has slowed rescue efforts, forcing crews to repeatedly pause work on unstable structures and landslide-blocked routes out of concern for further collapses.

Emergency responders have relied on heavy equipment to clear debris from roads connecting Flores' interior communities to coastal hospitals, but mountainous terrain and damaged infrastructure have made some areas reachable only on foot or by helicopter. Local authorities say the priority remains locating survivors, restoring access to remote villages, and delivering clean water, food, and medical supplies to displaced families.

## A Second Quake, Far Away

Hours after the Flores earthquake, a separate significant tremor struck near Sumatra, an island more than 2,000 kilometers to the west. While authorities have not linked the two events directly, the near-simultaneous disasters strained national resources already stretched thin by the Flores response, requiring BNPB to coordinate relief efforts across two regions at once.

Seismologists note that such back-to-back events, while striking in their timing, are not unusual for Indonesia, which straddles the Pacific Ring of Fire — a horseshoe-shaped zone stretching around the Pacific Basin where the majority of the world's earthquakes and volcanic eruptions occur. The archipelago sits at the junction of several tectonic plates, making seismic activity a near-constant feature of life for its more than 270 million residents.

## Testing a Familiar System Under New Strain

Indonesia has built one of the more experienced disaster-response frameworks in the world, shaped by decades of earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and the catastrophic 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. Early-warning networks, community evacuation drills, and rapid-deployment rescue units have all been refined in the years since. Even so, officials acknowledge that the combination of a high-magnitude quake, a prolonged aftershock sequence, and a second major event on the same day represents an unusually demanding scenario.

The government has mobilized military and volunteer personnel to support local first responders, while international aid organizations have begun coordinating with Indonesian authorities to assess additional needs. Officials caution that damage assessments are still ongoing and that casualty and displacement figures may continue to rise as rescue teams reach areas that remain cut off.

## What Comes Next

For now, the focus remains on the immediate humanitarian response: reopening roads, stabilizing damaged buildings, and ensuring displaced families have access to shelter and medical care as aftershocks continue to ripple through the region. Longer term, the disaster is expected to renew discussion around building codes, early-warning infrastructure, and preparedness funding in one of the most seismically active corridors on the planet — a reminder that for communities living along the Ring of Fire, resilience is not a one-time achievement but an ongoing effort.
